structured_checks.task: Code can be exported (GitHub or zip) and data downloaded
structured_checks.detail: run on 26 September 2026: the project zip export held the full source and its git history, but no database contents. Outside Replit it installed and built with pnpm 10 (pnpm 12 refused) once PORT and BASE_PATH were set, and ran against our own empty Postgres: schema created, a booking accepted and counted, admin login refused with a wrong password. sessions.what: Looked at by our team on 23 October 2026 in a demo account that RoverLead set up for us after contacting us: Daan logged in and our AI assistant explored it in Daan's browser. The campaigns, statistics and inbox conversations were RoverLead's own demo data. We did not connect LinkedIn and did not approve, resume or send anything, so no number on this page is a result of ours.
findings: Onboarding proposed an ideal customer profile from our own website: software development, IT services and business consulting, 1 to 200 employees, the Netherlands, UK, Ireland, US and Canada, founder, CEO, owner and managing-director titles, with government and education excluded. It then loaded 22 preview leads, each with a 'why now' signal: 13 a recent funding round (October 2026), 4 a new role and the rest recent activity.

Each lead in the demo campaign got a five-step sequence: a connection request without a note, then follow-ups 1, 3, 5 and 7 days later. Every message waited for Approve or Skip, with 'Approve all messages' and 'Generate 50 more' as bulk options.

The AI messages were tailored to us ('Drawn from 2 sources', including a comment the lead had made) and pitched our hands-on reviews and free listing, but also a '2026 B2B software stack guide' that we could not match to any existing page of ours. Read the drafts before you approve them.

After 'Looks good' the Lead Inbox said '21 leads found', one fewer than the 22 in the preview, with a signal per lead (new in role, recently active, recently funded), thumbs up or down for fit, and 'Connect LinkedIn' as the next setup step.

The Unibox sorted the 15 demo conversations into Starred, Hot, Nurture and Follow-up, with a 'Needs reply' filter. Opening one showed an AI reply marked 'Drafted · not sent' with a category; it only goes out when you click Send.
not_tested: Real sending through LinkedIn (not connected) and any acceptance or reply rate: the statistics in the demo account are RoverLead's demo data
How many actions a day RoverLead keeps to in practice
Editing the ideal customer profile, and lead quality outside the demo
Prices and trial terms inside the app (we read them on the website)

sessions.what: Tested by our team on 21 October 2026 on the free plan in Imagify's web app: Daan created the account and our AI assistant ran the test in Daan's browser. We uploaded three of our own simple test images (a 12 KB PNG, a 50 KB JPG and a 3.4 MB PNG), compared Smart and Lossless and watched the quota counter after each step.
findings: The account started at '0.0KB / 20MB used. You have 100% credit left.' Auto-converting PNG to JPEG is marked 'only for Pro users'; resizing is available on free.
Smart compression took the PNG from 11.8KB to 3.3KB (72.36%) and the JPG from 48.9KB to 12.3KB (74.91%), each within about 8 seconds.

After the first two images the quota counter read 61.44KB of 20MB, much closer to their input sizes than to the compressed results. The later counter increments varied, so we did not establish the exact quota accounting rule.
Lossless took the same PNG from 11.8KB to 5.8KB (51.05%), against 3.3KB with Smart.
The 3.4MB file was refused straight away with 'File size must be under 2.0 MB. Current file size is 3.4 MB' and used no quota.

The summary on the optimizer page is mislabelled: 'You saved 15.5KB out of 60.7KB' gave the size after compression (3.3KB + 12.3KB), while the real saving was about 45KB. The History page showed the right saving per file.
History notes 'Optimized images are available to download for 24 hours' on a free account. End state: 92.16KB of 20MB used after four optimisations and one refused upload.

The resize result (we did not check the output size)
The WordPress plugin and automatic WebP and AVIF conversion (we only used the web app)

sessions.what: A review account in SurFox's review sandbox, given to us by the founder. The sandbox says so on every page: leads, dashboards and results are sample data, messaging is switched off and the AI Learning page is a mock-up. Two things work for real there, the test conversation on a campaign and Surf, the campaign assistant. We played leads against a sample campaign for an analytics company over SMS on 3 October 2026, sent our findings to SurFox, and re-tested on 6 and 12 October 2026 after they shipped fixes. We did not send a real text, connect a CRM, take a voice call or see the learning feature work on real conversations.
findings: It did not invent a price. Asked what the product costs, the AI said the price depends on data sources and users and would be given on the call, which matched the knowledge document we gave it. A request to stop texting was honoured at once and classed as an opt-out.

The first test, on 3 October, had visible faults: a placeholder [SLOTS] sent as text, a summary claiming the lead had picked a time slot when they had not, a question answered as unknown although the knowledge document covered it, and openers longer than the 150 characters SurFox aims for. SurFox fixed these after our feedback. On 12 October the AI offered three real times, the booking produced a hot-lead email with a calendar file and a 20-minute duration that matched the conversation, and two openers came in at 143 and 130 characters.

Asking for a call directly ('Can someone call me this week?') ended the test as a hand-off to the team without offering a time; asking to book a demo did offer times. Both are reasonable, but you choose which one your campaign should push.

The learning feature that defines the Growth plan could not be judged: the sandbox shows sample data and says real learning needs hundreds of real conversations over several weeks. Delivery, voice, CRM syncing and real costs per conversation were also outside what a sandbox can show.
sessions.note: Findings as written up after the session; no pass/fail per task was scored.

findings: Onboarding has four steps: Train, Brand, Test and Install. Training sources are a website (with linked pages on the same domain, or a sitemap), files, text or YouTube, against a counter of '0 / 500K characters'. Our 177 characters of text were trained in about 10 to 20 seconds.

The guardrails slider starts on 'Max (default): Most sophisticated', which refuses off-topic questions and answers in the user's language; Chatwith warns that 'customizing or overriding the guardrails is difficult'.
All five fact questions were answered correctly, and four of the five rephrased ones, such as 'No. The Lila-17 is purple.' when we asked whether it was red.

Asked whether a fault after one month was covered by the 37-day warranty, it answered 'No. The Lila-17 warranty is 37 days, so it is still covered after one month.': it starts with no and ends with yes.

Asked about Sunday opening, which our text did not cover, it said 'I do not know the answer to this question.' and made nothing up. Our last question, on return costs, stayed at 'Not sent. Retry', also after a retry; we did not find out why.
The test chat made suggestion buttons from the knowledge itself (Product, Color, Pickup, Warranty) and shows 'Powered by Chatwith'.

findings: Signing up did not start on Free. The account landed on a Plus trial ('Trial Period Oct 20 - Nov 03', 1 user, $54/user, 'First monthly payment on Nov 4, 2026') plus a 92-day AI Answers trial, without asking for a payment card.

Switching to Free needed two clean-ups first. Free allows no private Docs site, so the empty knowledge base Help Scout had created had to be made public, and Free allows 0 workflows, so the two '[Try me]' example workflows had to be deleted. The confirmation screen then listed the Free limits, including 10 tags and 10 saved replies.

The 10-tag limit was not enforced right after the switch: an eleventh tag was accepted without any message and Settings > Tags showed '11 tags'. Only a lighter style on the conversation set it apart. Two of the ten were 'welcome' and 'practice', which Help Scout had created itself.

The 10-saved-reply limit was enforced, but with a generic error: 'Could not create saved reply draft' when opening a new one and 'Could not create saved reply' when saving, with no mention of a limit. An example reply Help Scout added counted as one of the ten.
Editing a saved reply worked: changing only the number of warranty days from 37 to 41 left the rest of the text unchanged after a reload.

Two phone notes for the same email address joined one customer profile, and the second showed the first in the sidebar. Help Scout filled in the company on its own ('Internet Assigned Numbers Authority' for example.com), and timestamps did not follow our Europe/Amsterdam time zone: 5:53 am was shown at 07:53 local time.

sessions.what: We did not summarise the marketing. Nextify.ai gave us Pro access for this test — disclosed here and in the video that goes with this review — and nothing else was agreed: no copy approval, and no draft shared before publication. On 7 September 2026 we generated a real ad from a product image inside that account, read the credit cost the app charges for every model it offers, and checked the pricing page both signed in and signed out. Everything below is what the product did and charged, not what the site says it does.
findings: Credits are charged per second of output, not per video. A four-second 720p clip on Seedance 2.0 — the model the editor pre-selects — cost 48 credits and took the balance from 3,000 to 2,952. The app's own credit table prices that combination at 12 a second, and the Generate button reads 48 before you commit, so the arithmetic is visible if you know to look for it.

Every tier's video count assumes 20 credits a video. Starter's 1,000 credits are sold as 50 videos, Pro's 3,000 as 150 and Business's 8,000 as 400 — all exactly 20 apiece, which is four seconds on the cheapest 5-credit-a-second model. On the model the editor actually opens with, Pro is 62 clips; at the 15-second maximum it is 16.

No image model costs what the image counts assume. Those counts work out at 2 credits an image on every tier, including the free one. The cheapest image model in the table is Nano Banana 2 at 1k for 7 credits, and the pre-selected GPT Image 2 is 10 — the button literally reads “Generate Image 10”. Starter's “up to 500 images” is about 100.

The avatar tools are the expensive ones, and they are the reason most people arrive. UGC Product Video and Lip-sync run on HeyGen AV4 at 6.7 credits a second, identical at 720p and 1080p, over 3 to 120 seconds. A 30-second avatar ad is 201 credits and a 60-second one is 402, so a Pro month is fourteen or seven of them.

Free users cannot reach the Seedance models at all. The model configuration marks seedance-2.0, seedance-2.0-fast and seedance-2.0-mini as unavailable on the free plan, so the 50 free credits run on Kling or MiniMax with a watermark — about two three-second clips.

“In seconds” is not what happens, but “three minutes” is fair. Our four-second clip took 126 seconds from submit to finished file, against the app's own on-screen estimate of four minutes. The homepage claim “Product Image to Viral Ad in 3 Minutes” holds up; the “in seconds” line on the same page does not.

The output was accurate to the prompt. We asked for a stainless steel insulated bottle on a kitchen counter in morning light, a hand picking it up, clean styling and no text overlay, and that is what came back — 9:16, 720p, four seconds, with generated audio. Nothing in the result argued against the tool; the argument is with the pricing page.
The pricing page hides the free plan once you sign in. Signed out, Free sits at the head of the ladder; signed in, the same URL starts at Starter.

sessions.what: Daan created the free account and logged in; everything after that was read inside the workspace on 11 September 2026 -- the credit screen, the plans and billing screen and the upgrade panel -- alongside Bitscale's own credit documentation. Two limits worth stating plainly. We did not run an enrichment: the grid renders in a canvas our browser panel could not drive, so the per-record credit costs below come from Bitscale's published credit table and not from a meter we moved ourselves. And Bitscale is an affiliate partner of ours; their partner manager offered 2,000 bonus credits that same morning, which had not been added when we looked -- the account was on the ordinary free allowance of 200, which is what a new reader gets.
findings: The free tier runs two meters, not one, and the account screen shows both: 200 platform credits and 2,000 search credits, each resetting monthly, with the next search reset dated on the page. Enriching a record spends platform credits; finding one through Find People or Find Companies spends a search credit, one per record. A reader budgeting on "200 credits" is reading half the meter, and it is the half that runs out first.

On Free, nothing carries over. The billing screen states it twice -- "Rolled-Over Credits: Not included in the plan" and "Rollover Limit: Not included in the plan" -- so an unused month is gone rather than banked. Rollover is listed among the things the first paid plan unlocks, next to credit rollover, the 100+ providers, action columns beyond 20 per grid, and the inbound integrations (RB2B, Factors, Vector).

What one enriched record costs is published, and the range is the whole story: one to twelve platform credits per successful email or phone lookup, depending on how many providers the waterfall is allowed to try. An AI enrichment is one to two credits a run, a BitAgent website scrape one per query, and anything arriving through the API is free. On Growth that turns 15,000 credits into anywhere between 1,250 and 15,000 enriched contacts -- 2.3 cents each at one credit, 28 cents at twelve.

The in-app upgrade panel carries a Growth benefit the public plan cards do not mention: three hours a quarter with a GTM engineer, alongside the 15,000 credits. Worth knowing before you compare the $349 against a pure data vendor, because it is consulting time rather than volume.

The two meters are set to become convertible. Bitscale's documentation announces 1 platform credit = 10 search credits as an upcoming feature, handled manually for enterprise accounts today. Until that ships, a month where you burn the enrichment pool cannot be topped up from the search pool, however much of it is left.

sessions.what: We did not read the docs and summarise them: PartnerStack is the platform our own affiliate operation runs on. We manage 58 partner programmes through it, pull the Partner API v2 on a schedule, and stamp sub-IDs across 704 pages of our own site. PartnerStack is also an affiliate partner of ours — we earn 15% of every sale for a year on anyone who signs up through our link — which is why the findings below are things we measured against our own records rather than claims from their marketing.
findings: A record in the customers endpoint is a tracked click, not a signup. One plain curl on a tracking link produced a customer record one second later, has_paid false, with no browser and no account. Records surface in the API about five minutes after the click, so allow ten before concluding a test did nothing.

Clicks arrive without a source. There is no referring-URL field in the partnership data, so the platform can tell you a link was clicked and never which page produced it. We had to build sub-ID stamping across our own pages to answer that question ourselves.

Commission terms do not come from the API. offers.base_rate is returned null on every partnership we hold. The readable source is PartnerStack's own public directory at market.partnerstack.com — and it sometimes contradicts the vendor's own affiliate page, which is worth knowing before you quote a rate to anyone.

Programme status lags the reality by days. One partner sent us a welcome email with a working tracking link on 7 August; the API still read application-denied and only turned active somewhere between 13 and 18 August. Treat the vendor's email as the leading indicator and the API status as the one that catches up.
The earned-commission endpoints are the weakest part. rewards and transactions did not return usable data for us, so what you have actually been paid is a dashboard question rather than an API one.

Partner replies break email threading. A partner answers inside the PartnerStack dashboard and the platform sends that on as a fresh message from hello@partnerstackmail.com, with a new Message-ID and no reference to the mail it is answering. Any automation of yours that matches replies to threads will not match these.

sessions.what: accessiBe's free accessScan scanner, not the paid accessWidget overlay this review prices. We built two versions of the same small landing page: one with 20 accessibility errors we placed on purpose and wrote down beforehand (missing page language and title, images without text alternatives, unlabelled form fields, low contrast, a skipped heading level, a table without header cells, a clickable div, a positive tabindex, an unlabelled iframe and more), and a twin with all 20 fixed. We scanned both and, as a reference, ran the free open-source checker axe-core 4.10.2 over the same two pages.
findings: The verdict was right both ways. The broken page came back 'Non-compliant' with 14 issues (10 critical, 3 serious, 1 moderate); the fixed twin came back 'Accessible'.

Of our 20 planted errors, the full report identified 7 correctly: the missing language, the empty title, the unlabelled button, the unlabelled iframe, aria-hidden on a link, the missing main landmark and the clickable div. An eighth, a link containing only an image without alt text, was flagged under the wrong diagnosis: the report called the image decorative and advised hiding it, which would leave the link with no name at all. axe-core found 13 of the same 20.

What it missed: the form had an email field and a dropdown without labels and a phone field labelled only by its placeholder, and the report's Forms category read 0. It also missed the image with no alt text, the alt text that was a filename, the low-contrast text, the skipped heading level, the table without header cells and the positive tabindex. For the filename alt text and the 'click here' link the report has a rule, but marked it 'Relevant: No'.

findings: Free gives 2 PNG downloads per account, not per design: the download panel went from '2 Downloads Left' to 1 and then 0 across two different designs. A third try opened 'You have run out of free downloads.' with 'Choose your plan', and no file came.

PNG is the only free file format. PDF and PowerPoint carry a BUSINESS label, and choosing PDF opened an upgrade window straight away. Normal, Medium and High quality were all open on Free; a transparent background asked for an upgrade.

The AI kept all three numbers ('Appels: 12', 'Peren: 8', 'Bananen: 20': apples, pears, bananas) but extended our title to 'TESTHAVEN Fruit Inventaris' and added sentences of its own ('Perfect voor een gezonde snack of in een taart', 'Perfect for a healthy snack or in a cake'). In the AI design's export the heading 'TOTAAL' in the closing block overlapped the paragraph below it, leaving part of it unreadable, and the photo next to 'Peren: 8' showed no pears.

sessions.what: We did not stop at the marketing. On 25 September 2026 we opened a free Jibble account (organisation 'AIBM hands-on test', web browser only), clocked in and out, invited a second user, exported a timesheet and opened the upgrade screen without buying anything. Nothing was agreed with Jibble about this test. Everything below is what the product did and showed, not what the site says.
findings: The account lands on Free at €0, marked as the selected plan, with a 14-day trial of the paid features running alongside it. During those two weeks nothing is locked, so what you see in week one is more than Free keeps.

The price table exists, just not on the public site. The upgrade button opens four plans with annual and monthly prices (euros, excluding VAT, as shown from the Netherlands): Free €0; Essentieel €1.79 or €2.99; Groei €3.79 or €4.99; Pro €6.79 or €9.29 per user a month. No demo form and no sales call in between.

Jibble's own plan comparison, one click further, answers what Free excludes: no timesheet approval workflow, no automatic break deductions or custom pay periods, no smart reminders, alerts or automatic clock-out, no groups, one admin, two locations, one work schedule and one kiosk, and no attendance report, leave workflow or leave balances. Free keeps overtime calculations, face recognition, selfie, PIN and NFC clock-ins, GPS-verified clock-ins and geofences, timesheet and report exports, and the Slack, Microsoft Teams, QuickBooks Online, Xero, Deel and Zapier integrations.
Setting up the organisation requires a phone number; the form will not continue without one. The marketing opt-in on the sign-up form is ticked by default.
Clocking out in the same minute you clocked in is refused, with a message saying you cannot clock out before clocking in. Jibble records whole minutes; two minutes later it worked.
Inviting a second member took a name and an email address and went through without any prompt to pay. The member shows as pending until they accept.

The weekly timesheet export offers XLS or CSV. Our CSV arrived within seconds and carries 32 columns per member per day, including worked hours, paid and unpaid breaks, deductions, payroll hours, daily and weekly overtime and billable amounts.
We did not switch on face recognition or GPS. The comparison puts both in Free; anti-spoofing, device lock and live location tracking are Pro only.

sessions.what: Daan started the 30-day trial; everything after that was measured inside the account. The first question the protocol asked was whether the trial takes a card, because their pricing page does not say. It does not — but the answer is on the signup page, not the pricing page, which is a small lesson in where vendors put the reassuring sentence.
findings: No card for the trial. The signup page states it plainly — “Try it free for 30 days. No credit card required. Cancel anytime.” — and the form asks only for an email address and a password. The pricing page, where you would actually look, says nothing about it.

The prices inside the account are not the prices on the pricing page. The public page leads with the promotional rate, currently a limited-time 90% off for three months. The in-app upgrade screen quotes the real thing: Lite $23, Plus $43, Premium $70 a month, with a Yearly toggle marked “Save 10%”. Sign up on the strength of $2.30 and the first screen you see afterwards is $23.
Two add-ons ride along on every tier, and they are easy to miss: Team Members at $11 per user a month, and Advanced Payments at $20 a month. They are listed under Lite, Plus and Premium alike.

Removing FreshBooks branding from the emails your client receives is not a paid feature — it is a quote-only one. It appears only on the top “Let's Talk” tier, alongside lower card fees and two included team members. On Lite, Plus and Premium your invoice mail carries their brand.

The client ceiling that decides the tier is not testable during the trial. Lite stops at 5 clients, Plus at 50, Premium unlimited — but the trial runs with full features, as the upgrade screen says in as many words (“Upgrade to a paid plan to continue using all of FreshBooks' great features”). We fed the client importer a six-client CSV and it accepted the file and moved straight to field matching, with no limit warning at the point where a Lite account would have stopped. So the meter that will actually bite you is the one you cannot feel while you are evaluating.
Prices are shown in USD on a Netherlands account, and the plan screen carries the note “Features vary by region.”

sessions.what: We already knew from their pricing pages that Glide sells two products. What we had never done is the thing a reader does: go to glideapps.com and press the free signup button. Daan created the account; everything after that was measured in the product.
findings: The free signup button does not lead to the product our pricing section describes. Both “Sign up” and “Get started” on glideapps.com point at os.glideapps.dev — GlideOS. We signed up and landed there. The classic builder, with the free tier of unlimited drafts, one editor and 25k rows, sits behind glideapps.com/classic, which you only reach if you already know to look for it.

The two ladders are an order of magnitude apart. Classic business pricing starts at $199 a month billed yearly; GlideOS Basic is $25 a month. Same brand, same homepage, two different products with two different price floors.

And the meter is different. Classic bills updates — 5,000 included, 2 cents each after that. GlideOS bills credits: Basic 100 a month, Plus 250, Pro 500 and upward with team size. So the “updates, not seats” warning that applies to Classic does not describe the product a new signup actually lands in.

GlideOS's free tier publishes no number. Every paid tier lists its credit allowance; the free column says “Limited credits”, alongside 2 team members and 10 projects. Nowhere in the app is there a balance — not on the dashboard, not in the account menu, not on the upgrade screen. You cannot find out what you have or what you have spent.

The AI itself is not walled off on free. From one sentence — “build a simple app to track software subscriptions” — it drew up a plan, asked a sensible clarifying question about where the data lives today, produced a working mockup and then began importing components one by one. We hit no credit wall during any of it.

sessions.what: The free plan, on a test landing page of our own with PagePulse's tracking script pasted before </body>, as its setup screen instructs. We then sent scripted visits whose every detail we logged: 10 visitors in 11 sessions (one came back in a new tab), 4 arriving from google.com, 3 from x.com and the rest direct, 3 on a phone-sized screen, 6 clicks on 'Start free trial', 3 clicks on 'Book a demo' that led to a second page, and visits of 35, 20 or 5 seconds. A second, smaller run of 3 visitors with one click each followed later, with every message the script sent logged. We compared the dashboard with what we had done.
findings: The counts were right. Visitors 10 and page views 14 matched exactly, as did the source split (Google 4, X 3, direct 4 of 14 views) and the device split (3 mobile, 7 desktop). In the second run every number moved by exactly what we sent: visitors 10 to 13, page views 14 to 17, 'Start free trial' clicks up by exactly 3.
Clicks on links and buttons are captured without extra setup and named by their text ('Start free trial', 'Book a demo'). The script itself sent one event per click.

Engagement does not follow its own definition. The tooltip defines an engaged session as one lasting 10+ seconds, with 2+ page views, or a conversion. By that rule 8 of our first 11 sessions qualify, as they lasted 20 to 35 seconds. The dashboard showed 27%: exactly the 3 sessions with two page views. The 20-second sessions of the second run did not count either.
A click from our page to our own thank-you page shows up as a traffic source, listed as the site's own domain at 21% next to Google and X.

The 'Here's what we found' analysis was general copywriting advice drawn from the page text (move the call to action, add testimonials), not from the visit data, and it sat under the line 'Once your tracking is set up', while tracking demonstrably worked.

The free script records page views, clicks, time on page through a ping every 15 seconds, and load times. It does not record scroll depth, and conversions need your own trackConversion call, which the dashboard says is part of Starter and above.

sessions.what: Two sessions on the free plan. On 7 September we ran it by hand: Daan logged in, and we read every counter against a test file of exactly five minutes that we built inside the page; Descript was not a partner of ours then and contributed nothing. On 30 September, by then a PartnerStack partner, we drove Descript from Claude through Descript's connector, for Descript's partner content challenge, which pays the first five entries $250: we uploaded one of our own five-minute review videos and asked for vertical clips in plain sentences, once directly and once from a claude.ai chat.
findings: The free plan's 100 AI credits are one-time, not monthly. Descript says so itself in two places: the plan card reads "100 AI credits at signup" for Free against "400 AI credits / month" for Hobbyist, and the usage screen inside the app puts "Lifetime AI credits used 0/100" next to "Monthly media minutes used 0/60". That pair of words -- lifetime against monthly -- is the whole answer.

Media minutes come off at IMPORT, not at export, and per minute of media. Two five-minute files took the counter from 60m to 50m. Their own upload dialog says it too: "Each file added uses media minutes". Exporting costs no minutes and no credits, according to Descript itself.

The AI assistant, Underlord, charges per instruction, and it does run on the free plan. Importing and transcribing cost 3 credits, Studio Sound over a ten-minute track 9 credits, and a question about the export settings 6 credits.

An instruction that returns nothing still costs credits. "Remove all filler words" answered "No filler words were found -- the script shows 0 words, so there's nothing to remove" and deducted 2 credits anyway.
Five instructions without a single real edit spent 20 of the 100 one-time credits. Anyone using the free plan as a trial is through it in an afternoon, and no more arrive.

Studio Sound ran on Free, while the pricing table presents it as a Hobbyist benefit ("Studio Sound, Remove Filler Words, Create Clips, and more"). The line "Limited use of Underlord" on the free card is therefore more generous than the comparison table suggests.
In onboarding, the consent "Our team analyzes your project information" is TICKED BY DEFAULT, in a step most people click straight through. You can turn it off, but you have to do it yourself.
The watermark on the free plan sits in the bottom right of the frame; paid plans do not have it.

Through Claude's Descript connector, a 5:15 review video of ours (94 MB) uploaded and transcribed in about 30 seconds. The import used 315 media seconds, consistent with minutes being charged at import.

One sentence to Underlord through Claude (a vertical 9:16 clip of about 30 seconds on the price and the 90-day data limit, with captions, keeping the words and numbers as spoken) produced a new 24-second vertical composition in two and a half minutes for 48.3 AI credits. The original composition was left untouched, and the clip's transcript matched the source word for word, numbers included.

From a claude.ai chat, Claude asked permission before each Descript action, read the transcript itself, chose the passage from 01:15 to 01:40 and had Underlord cut a 21-second vertical clip with burned-in captions in about three minutes. It also fixed the transcript's misspelling of the product name in the captions and said that it had.

The vertical version is a centre crop. On our 16:9 video it cut off the text card at the side of the frame, and because our video already carries subtitles, Descript's captions landed on top of them. Ask for the full frame on a blurred background, and skip added captions when your source already has them.

Our request to fix that was refused because the free plan had run out of AI credits: the one-time 100 were gone after our first session plus these two edits. Real editing work through Claude needs a paid plan.

Publishing gave an unlisted share link and an MP4 download in about a minute and a half. We asked for 1080p and received 720x1280 with the watermark in the bottom right, so the 720p cap on the Free plan card is what applies, not the 4K that Descript's own assistant named in our first session.

sessions.what: We ran the import ourselves instead of summarising Capsule's help pages. Daan created the account; everything after that was measured in the product. We built a deliberately messy CSV — 24 rows, one row repeated with a different job title and phone number, and one row carrying nothing but an organisation name — imported it with “Import and update duplicates” and the overwrite box ticked, and then tried to undo it. The account was a fresh one on the 14-day premium trial, so nothing below is a free-plan restriction.
findings: 24 rows became 34 contacts. Capsule creates a separate Organisation record for every distinct organisation name in the file — 22 people plus 12 organisations. Nobody warns you, and it matters: the free plan stops at 250 contacts, so a 24-row spreadsheet costs 34 of them.
A row with only the Organisation column filled does build a company record on its own. Our “Solitary Holdings BV” row arrived as an organisation with its phone number attached.

The duplicate row wins. Anna Bakker went in twice, second time as “Head of Marketing” instead of “Marketing Lead”, and the record ended up with the later title. So the last occurrence in the file overwrites the earlier one, inside a single import.

But “overwrite” means exactly the four fields it names — name, job title, organisation and custom fields — and nothing else. The two rows carried different phone numbers and the contact now holds BOTH, sitting side by side. Contact channels are appended, not replaced, so a bad update pass leaves duplicate numbers on the record rather than wrong ones.

We could not find an undo or bulk-delete action in the screens we checked during this trial. The import history logs '34 total imported, 34 contacts created' and offers View and Close; View opens a saved filter with those 34 contacts, whose bulk actions were Tag, Create Campaign and Export. We found no delete on that list, on the full contact list, on the contact record or on its edit screen.
We did not establish that Capsule has no recovery route. Test a small import first and check the available rollback options before updating real contacts.

sessions.what: A 14-day trial of Freshservice for Business Teams on the Pro plan, set up for an HR team. Note the variant: this is Freshworks' service desk for HR, finance and facilities, priced separately from the IT edition whose plans this review lists. We sent six HR requests by email to the desk's default address: a missing payslip, a parental-leave request with a date, 'URGENT: my salary was not paid today' (rent due tomorrow), a request to change the bank account for salary payments, a remote-work policy question, and the payslip email a second time as a duplicate. We changed no default setting first, so this is what a team gets on day one.
findings: Email-to-ticket worked: all six emails became tickets (CASE-1 to CASE-6) within seconds, and the sender got a 'Ticket Received' confirmation for each within the same minute.

Every ticket came in at priority Low with the same deadlines: first response by 13 October, five days and seven hours after we wrote, and resolution by 20 October. That includes the unpaid-salary email, which the subject line itself marked URGENT. Out of the box nothing reads urgency from the text; you have to build rules for it.

Freddy AI Copilot, available in the Pro trial, summarised the urgent ticket correctly in two lines and named the urgency ('an urgent need as his rent is due tomorrow'). The summary did not change the priority or the deadline: the AI saw what the triage did not act on.
The duplicate was not caught. The second identical payslip email opened its own ticket, and its Related tickets tab read 'No related tickets yet'.
The bank-account change, a request payroll teams treat as a fraud risk, was handled like any other ticket: same priority, no verification step, no flag.

sessions.what: A new free account, with no payment method asked for. We ran nine texts whose authorship we knew before we started: three passages from public-domain books (Darwin and William James), a paragraph one of us typed for the test, typos included, three paragraphs a language model wrote for our own reviews, one paragraph Claude wrote on the spot, and one of those machine paragraphs with three of its five sentences rewritten by Claude. We read the credit meter after every check and ran it into the daily limit.
findings: Nine for nine. All four human texts came back 'Human Written', including the 71-word paragraph typed for the test, and all five machine texts came back 'AI Generated', including the paragraph Claude wrote on the spot. Every result put the whole text on one side: the gauge read 100% each time. That figure is the share of the text it assigns to each side, not a confidence score.

A machine rewrite did not shake it. With three of its five sentences rewritten by a second model, the paragraph from our Hubstaff review still scored 100% AI. That measures a model paraphrasing a model; we did not test text a person had edited by hand.

Later the same day we gave it a tenth text: a deliberately clichéd AI paragraph after QuillBot's AI Humanizer had rewritten it (the Humanizer reported '0 AI signals'). Pangram still scored it 100% AI and added a note that the text 'appears to have been paraphrased or rewritten', pointing to one rewritten segment. Our own Claude rewrite of a review paragraph, earlier in the test, did not get that note.

Short texts carry a caveat, and very short ones are refused. Every text of 190 words or fewer was marked 'Confidence limited — short text'; the 224-word passage was not. Below 50 words the button stays grey, with 'Minimum 50 words required for accurate detection', and nothing is charged.

The 2,000 words a day are 20 credits of 100 words, rounded up per check. A 190-word text cost 2 credits and a 222-word text cost 3. Our first six checks came to 1,014 words and used 13 credits, the allowance for 1,300 words. At around 150 words a check, a day holds ten checks, not twenty. The cost shows next to the button before you click, and the balance sits at the top of the page.

The window does not say when the credits come back, and it does not offer to trim the text to what you have left.
Signed in and signed out, the pricing page shows the same amounts. The Professional button now reads 'Upgrade to Professional', with '$65 billed now' underneath, so that tier still has no trial.

sessions.what: A new free account in ngram's v2 studio. We pasted the link to one of our own published reviews (ActiveCampaign) with a one-line brief, asked for 30 seconds, ran the same prompt twice and read the credit meter before and after each run.
findings: The new account opened with 1,200 credits, while ngram's pricing page (read the same day) lists the Free plan at 600 one-time credits. We report what the meter showed; we do not know why it was double.

The composer states the rate plainly: 10 credits a second, billed on the generated duration. It reserved 300 credits for a 30-second request, but both videos came out slightly long, at 32.5 and 32 seconds, and were charged 330 and 320 credits. The meter went 1,200 to 870 to 550, matching those charges exactly. The 32.5-second video was charged 330 credits, equivalent to 33 seconds at the displayed rate; we did not establish the rounding rule.

From the link alone it read the page, picked up the site's own colours, type and logo, and wrote a scene-by-scene storyboard with the narration script in about a minute and a half. Nothing was charged until we approved that plan, which is the moment to catch a wrong claim.

Every figure in both scripts matched the review: $15 a month as the floor, and $149, $189, $375 and $589 at 10,000 contacts, as read on 29 September 2026. It declined to animate prices between those two points because the review does not print them, and it kept the review's attribution on the contact-billing rule (credited to SendX in one run, labelled as reported in the other).

The same prompt gave a different video each time: five scenes in the first run, four in the second, with different wording and visuals. The facts stayed the same, but do not expect a repeat run to reproduce a video you liked.

Rendering took about six to seven and a half minutes after approval. The narration step failed once in each run and recovered on its own, and the second run said openly that it could not listen to its own voice-over and flagged one word that might sound clipped. Listen before you publish.

The visuals were motion graphics: the log showed ngram writing the scenes as an HTML animation and recording that, not generated camera footage. That suits explainers and product walkthroughs; it is not the tool for filmed-looking scenes.
Videos are private by default; sharing offers a public link, an embed, a download and direct posting to LinkedIn, X and YouTube, and captions are included.

sessions.what: We built a support agent from scratch with the description 'A customer support agent for Acme Headsets that answers customer questions using the attached help centre page', and gave it one public help-centre page of our own as its only knowledge: shipping countries and times, a 15:00 dispatch cut-off, returns, warranty, spare parts, two headsets with prices and support hours, with no phone line. We asked 13 questions, each in a new conversation on the agent's standalone chat page: ten the page answers, and three it does not (Japan, PayPal, and battery life with noise cancelling on). The first round ran without an account; after about ten conversations it stopped with 'This AI Agent has reached its conversation limit', so the last three, plus two repeats, ran on a new agent built the same way in a free Starter account.
findings: Eleven of 13 answers were right. Delivery times, the free-shipping threshold, the return window, free returns, the warranty exclusion, spare-part and headset prices and the 40-hour battery figure all matched the page.

It did not make things up when the page had no answer. It said it could not confirm PayPal, gave the 40-hour figure only for noise cancelling off and said it had no figure for it on, and inferred correctly that it does not ship to Japan because only the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany are listed.

It got the dispatch cut-off wrong. Asked about an order at 4 pm on a Tuesday, the first agent said it would not ship that day but not when it would; the second said it would ship the same day, because orders before 15:00 leave that day. The correct answer is Wednesday. The same question gave a different answer on a near-identical agent.

Asked 'Can I call you?', both agents said a representative had been asked to join and asked for an email address, instead of saying there is no phone support. With no live team behind it, that promise goes nowhere.
Adding the page once showed '2 links' in the knowledge base both times. The guest agent's conversation limit arrived after about ten chats; the free Starter plan lists 100 conversations a month.

sessions.what: A new free Basic account. We made one 29-second video from a blank template with a stock avatar and our own 99-word script, read the credit meter on the Billing page before and after, then changed one word and generated it again. The same day we compared the app's upgrade window with the public pricing page.
findings: Onboarding knew who we were before we told it. We skipped the company-website question, yet the prompt box was pre-filled with a brief about our own site, with suggestions such as 'Introduce the Tool Finder', and four draft videos about us appeared in the library without being asked for. They used no credits.

The meter charges by the second. Our 29-second video took the Billing page from 0 to 59 of 1,200 credits, about 2 credits a second, and the app's banner went from '600 seconds' to '571 seconds of video creation time left'. In this account the free month is 10 minutes of finished video. The public pricing page the same day prices video at 100 credits a minute, which would make 59 credits about 35 seconds.

A small edit did not cost the whole video again. After changing one word and generating again, the meter moved from 59 to 63 credits. The second time, though, the button read 'Generate in 15 minutes' instead of 'Generate' and the job went into a queue. Each version took about eight to nine minutes from the click to a finished video.
An upgrade window ('You only have 600 seconds of video creation time left') opened the moment we clicked Generate, and again on every reload of the video page.

On Basic the video carries the Synthesia logo. 'Remove watermark' is marked as paid in the Generate window, and the Billing page lists 'Download your videos' as a Starter feature; we did not try to download.

The app and the public pricing page described different plans on the same day. The app's upgrade window offered Starter at €19 a month or €12 billed yearly with 15,500 credits a year, and Creator at €79 or €49 with 72,500 credits a year. The public pricing page, read without signing in and served in dollars, lists Starter at $29 or $18 with 1,250 credits a month and a Pro plan at $89 or $64 with 6,000 credits a month where Creator used to be; its own comparison table still says 'Free, Starter, and Creator'.
The AI Assistant page that should have built a video from our prompt stayed on a loading screen for over 90 seconds in our session, so we built the video from a blank template instead.

sessions.what: A free account, used on QuillBot's AI Detector, AI Humanizer and Paraphraser. We ran the detector over the texts of known authorship we used for our Pangram test the same day: three passages from public-domain books, a paragraph one of us typed for the test, three paragraphs a language model wrote for our own reviews, and one Claude wrote on the spot. We added a control paragraph written in stock chatbot phrasing, sent it through the Humanizer, and checked the rewrite in QuillBot's detector and in Pangram.
findings: The detector scored all eight texts 0% AI, the four machine-written ones included. Our three review paragraphs and the paragraph Claude wrote on the spot each came back '100% Human-written'. Pangram, given the same eight texts the same day, labelled every one correctly.

It does catch AI text that sounds like AI. The control paragraph, which opens “In today's fast-paced digital landscape”, scored 100% AI, with the stock phrases underlined and the opening sentence listed as 'High'. In our test it picked up the style, not the authorship: plainly written machine text passed as human.

The Humanizer and the detector disagree. The Humanizer rewrote the control paragraph and reported '0 AI signals' on its own output. QuillBot's detector scored that same output 100% AI. Pangram scored it 100% AI too and added that it 'appears to have been paraphrased or rewritten'. The rewrite mostly swapped words: 'seamless' became 'smooth', 'In conclusion' became 'Simply put'.
Every result came with the prompt 'Want your text to sound more authentic? Refine with Paraphraser', including on texts the detector had just rated 100% human.

Signed out, the detector ran four checks (689 words) and then asked us to sign up. It will not run below 40 words, and under 80 it shows 'For more accurate results, add at least 80 words'; it still scored our 71-word paragraph.

The free Paraphraser's 125-word cap is real, and stricter than it sounds. Given 219 words, it reported '219/125 words. Limit exceeded' and showed only the first sentence of the rewrite, with the rest blurred behind an upgrade button, not the first 125 words.
The detector page showed model version v7.1.0.
not_tested: Premium, the plagiarism and grammar checkers, the Humanizer's daily use limit, languages other than English and texts longer than 219 words

sessions.what: The Freddy AI Agent in a Freshchat trial account, built in AI Agent Studio. We wrote a short help page for a made-up headset shop (shipping, returns, warranty, two products, opening hours: about 250 words) and gave the agent its URL as the only knowledge source; learning finished in about two minutes. We then ran 13 customer questions through the studio's Test screen: 10 whose answer is on the page, one that needs a small inference (shipping to Japan when the page lists only three countries) and two whose answer is not on the page at all (PayPal, and battery life with noise cancelling on). We scored every reply against the page.
findings: 11 of the 13 replies were correct, and every factual reply linked the help page as its source. That includes the trickier ones: an order at 4pm on a Tuesday ships on Wednesday because of the 15:00 cut-off, a cable broken by pulling is excluded from the warranty, and 'Do you ship to Japan?' got a clear no with the three countries we do ship to.

It did not invent anything where the page was silent. Asked about PayPal, it said the help centre has no information on payment methods. Asked for battery life with noise cancelling on, it gave the documented 40 hours, said that figure is with noise cancelling off, and declined to give a number for the other case.

The one wrong reply was 'Can I call you?'. The page says there is no phone support; the agent answered 'Sure! Assigning your chat to our support agent.' It treated the question as a request for a human and started a handover, and the 'Sure!' reads as a yes. The Test dashboard still counted this reply as Answered.
One reply added something the page does not contain: after correctly refusing the warranty claim, it offered to explain 'replacing the cable at your own cost', which our page never mentions.

The dashboard's totals (12 answered, 1 unanswered) are a useful first filter, but you have to read the replies: the handover counted as an answer, and the correct 'I don't know' about PayPal counted as unanswered.

Its own test booked one person at a time. When we sent ten bookings for an empty eight-spot class at the same moment, all ten were accepted, after which the class list returned an error and the public page showed 'No classes on the calendar yet.' until two bookings were cancelled.

Given that exact description, the Agent added a database lock per class in two minutes; the same ten simultaneous bookings then gave exactly eight. The same repair stopped it accepting a name made only of spaces.

On Starter the usage page is closed ('You must have an active subscription to view your own usage'), so you cannot see what a request cost, and the daily allowance was gone after the build and one repair.
The code export, run from the project zip, built and ran outside Replit on our own database, but the export and its Git history carried the generated admin password in plain text.

findings: Prezi's AI editor opened in a pop-up window and built ten slides plus its zooming overview in under four minutes, using 150 of the 500 starting credits.

It added no numbers of its own and drew both charts to scale, but it made up a company website (kettlecrumb.nl), gave the CEO a gender the brief did not, and described 2025's actual revenue as a projection.
Asked once to 'Change the ask to €450,000 for 12%', it updated the ask slide but left 'Our €400,000 investment' on the use-of-funds slide, so the deck contradicted itself.

sessions.what: We did not just read the docs: we ran 40 pricing queries across 20 tools and two engines through the async batch endpoint for a research report of our own, then spent a further handful of credits measuring what individual requests actually cost. Cloro is an affiliate partner of ours, which is why we checked their credit table against the meter instead of quoting it.
findings: A plain async ChatGPT task billed 5 credits, not the 7 the pricing table lists for a full ChatGPT response — that is the web-search rate. It held over 20 requests in a batch and again on a single measured call. Budget from 5 and the free tier is 100 ChatGPT answers, not 71.

The credit meter lags. Straight after a completed ChatGPT task the balance was unchanged; the charge landed about 90 seconds later. If you gate your own spending on a balance read immediately after a call, you will overshoot.

The harvest does not echo your request back: task.payload comes back null. Submit a batch of 40 and nothing in the response tells you which answer belongs to which query — you have to keep your own map of task id to question. This cost us a wrong result on the first pass.

The response shape differs per engine, so there is no single schema to code against. ChatGPT returned text, sources, citationPills and model; Perplexity returned no model but added related_queries, search_model_queries and shopping_cards.
Async tasks came back in roughly 30 to 40 seconds each, and on the free tier's single concurrent job a 40-task batch is a queue, not a burst — budget wall-clock time as well as credits.
Source counts swing wildly and that is the engine, not the API: one Perplexity call returned 10 sources, while in our 20-tool batch 14 of 20 Perplexity answers returned no sources at all.

sessions.what: The free plan on a new account. We uploaded one recording whose exact script we hold: the 2-minute-49 audio of our own Contabo video review, two synthetic voices and 377 words with prices, dates and product names. We compared the transcript word for word with the script, checked how it split the speakers, and read the AI summary and action items against what was said. In setup we chose the narrowest meeting settings: join only meetings we invite it to, recaps to the account owner only.
findings: The transcript was close: after evening out punctuation and number formats, 5.3% of the 377 words differed from the script. Product names such as Contabo, DigitalOcean, Cloud VPS 12, cPanel and Plesk came through.

The errors sat where a buyer would care. '6.70 euros a month' came out as '6.€70amonth', 'the usual fine print' as 'the US fine print', and 'excluding VAT' dropped out of the sentence with the entry price, though a later sentence kept 'Prices on the page exclude vat'.
Speaker detection found six speakers in a recording with two voices, and split single sentences across them.

The AI summary had the facts right: the 24-month prepaid term, about 25% more month to month, backups at 6.70 euros and the DigitalOcean comparison. Its one action item was assigned to 'Daniel Cho', a name that is not spoken anywhere in the recording.

The free plan's 'unlimited transcription' depends on your settings. In setup the switch for unlimited free transcripts sits beside the line 'Users on Join-All and Share-All settings get unlimited meeting transcripts': Fireflies joining every meeting with a link and sending recaps to everyone on the invite. Our narrower choice switched it off, and the account then showed '3 Free meetings'.
Right after the upload the app offered a 7-day Business trial, noting that billing may increase with usage once credits run out. We declined it, and the file was transcribed on the free plan.

sessions.what: We opened a new Databox account through the 'Get started' button under the Free plan on databox.com/pricing, connected Google Analytics 4 and Google Search Console for our own site, asked Genie two questions about that data, let Genie try to build a dashboard, and read the credit meter under Settings → Billing after every step. One account, one evening, our own traffic data — not a month of team use.
findings: The Free button does not give you Free. The account opened as a 14-day trial of Team Core at $249 a month, billed monthly. Free was listed in the app as a 'Downgrade'. Databox's own FAQ says that if no payment details are added by the end of the trial, syncing stops and reports pause, so anyone who wanted Free has to downgrade by hand before day 14.

The downgrade was blocked until we deleted Databox's own sample data. The message: 'You have 1 connected Spreadsheets, but the Free plan is limited to 0.' That one spreadsheet was the Sample dataset Databox adds at sign-up. Free allows no spreadsheets at all: Excel and Google Sheets both open an 'Upgrade to Analyst' wall at $89 a month, something the pricing page does not say.

Your one free dashboard is already taken. Databox's own Sample Dashboard stays after the downgrade and fills the plan's single dashboard slot. 'Create New Databoard' opened the $89 upgrade wall, and so did the button that would hang the sample dashboard on your own data.

What a Genie question costs: 3.7 credits for a simple one ('which pages got the most views in August'), 3.8 for a heavier week-by-week comparison. On Free's 50 a month that is about thirteen questions. The onboarding had already spent 1.9 credits by sending our four setup answers to Genie as a first question we never asked, and the app showed 'Buy more to keep Genie running' at 48 left.

Genie spends credits on things the plan will not allow. It offered to build a dashboard, tried three times, reported that Databox 'rejected the request as invalid' without naming the one-dashboard limit, and charged 5.2 credits for nothing. After one hour we had used 14.6 of the month's 50 credits.

Genie's diagnoses need checking. It called a half-finished Search Console connection 'broken' because 'the login expires' (the data manager said 'Unfinished connection'), and it flagged one of our real review URLs as a typo. The traffic figures themselves came back fast and were usefully broken down, including pages counted twice because of query strings.

What held up: connecting a data source cost no credits, the unfinished connection still counted against the three-source limit, and the plan prices inside the app matched the public pricing page ($89 / $249 / $399 monthly; $71 / $199 / $319 billed annually).
sessions.not_tested: We did not add a fourth data source past the limit, did not build our own dashboard after deleting the sample one, and could not check how fresh each source's data is: the app shows sync frequency but no last-synced time.

sessions.what: Tested by our team on 23 October 2026 on our existing Free account (the publication we use for our weekly mail, 3 subscribers), as a draft only: our AI assistant ran the test in Daan's browser. We wrote a post with a title and three known lines, checked all four previews and walked through every publishing step without sending or publishing anything.
findings: New > Blank draft post opened the editor (Compose, Audience, Email, Web, Review) in about 10 seconds. Above the editor sat a block 'Earn revenue with this newsletter! Upgrade to the Lite plan to claim them'.

The title and all three lines came through unchanged in all four previews (email and web, desktop and mobile): 0 field errors in 4 previews. The email preview used the title as subject and left the preview text empty; the web preview said '2 min read' for 12 words.
The Review step listed 'Fix before you publish: Add email preview text', next to Send test email and Schedule. We sent nothing.

Audience offers Email and web, Email only or Web only, defaulting to all subscribers. The Email step has subject, preview text, sender name, UTM settings and custom headers; the Web step has the post URL, thumbnail and SEO title and description (defaulting to the publication description). 'Audio newsletter' was available only with Pro.

We could not find a way to create a second, separate publication on the Free plan: not in the sidebar or the New menu, and /publications/new returned a 404. That is why we tested as a draft in the existing publication.
After Exit without publishing, Posts listed the draft with its last-edited time; the subscriber count stayed at 3 and no new send appeared.
not_tested: Actually sending, deliverability and open rates
A separate second publication on the Free plan
Importing subscribers, the growth network (Boosts), the Ad Network and paid subscriptions
The website builder and a custom domain
The difference between Free and Lite or Pro beyond the visible locks (Ad Network claims, audio newsletter)

sessions.what: Tested by our team on 21 October 2026 during the 14-day trial, without a card and without connecting accounting software or a bank: Daan created the account and our AI assistant ran the test in Daan's browser. We uploaded two made-up receipts whose every field we knew, then a byte-identical copy of one and a rotated copy of the other.
findings: Both receipts reached the Costs inbox within about a minute, and all eight fields we checked were right: date, supplier, total and tax on each (EUR 12.10 with EUR 2.10 tax, and EUR 21.80 with EUR 1.80 tax). Dext picked the category itself: 'Office Supplies' for the stationery receipt and 'Travel' for the transport one.
The rotated copy was marked 'Duplicate' in Submission history and kept out of the inbox, which is right, but it still counted: the usage counter went from 0 to 3 of 250 for two receipts.
The byte-identical copy appeared nowhere, not even in Submission history: it was dropped without a message.

The workspace worked straight away without any connection. Onboarding asked three questions (industry, company size and accounting software, with Spreadsheets as an option); the overview showed 'Documents extracted 0 / 250, Resets in 1 days' and trial credits for 10 bank statement, 5 supplier statement and 5 line-item extractions, 5 Vault AI credits and 500 MB of Vault storage.

Upload offers one document per file (PDF, JPG, PNG, ZIP), one per page (PDF) or auto-splitting (PDF, 'Can take up to 1 hour'), with limits of 6 MB per image or PDF, 100 MB per ZIP and 40 MB for an auto-split PDF. Each account also gets its own email address for sending in documents.

sessions.what: Historical test data: these are measurements from 4 September 2026, at that day's free allowance and meters, not today's Free plan or the standard cost of every Bot. We ran the reproducible test BrowserAct's own partner team proposed, on a free account with the 1,500 sign-up credits the card offered at the time. The prompt, verbatim: open books.toscrape.com, collect the first 20 books in listing order, open each detail page and return full title, displayed price, availability and source URL, leave unavailable fields blank, infer nothing. Before touching BrowserAct we fetched the same 20 pages with plain HTTP and saved the four fields as ground truth, so every value below was checked against the source, not against BrowserAct's own claims. Then we built the Bot from the prompt, ran it twice from the published version, and read the credit meter after each step.
findings: Accuracy: 80 of 80 fields correct, three times over. The build's own verification output, run 1 and run 2 each returned 20 rows with title, price, availability and URL identical to our ground truth, including the parenthetical stock counts ('In stock (22 available)') and the currency symbol, which the Bot kept as displayed rather than converting.

The build costs more than the runs. Building the Bot took 4 minutes 59 seconds and 278 credits; the agent inspected the listing and a detail page, wrote a small package (a SKILL.md, a run.py and two DOM helpers), compiled it, and ran it end to end before declaring it ready. On that day's free tier that was about a fifth of the sign-up credits spent before the first real run. The pricing page now estimates 300 to 500 credits for a simple Agent build, and today's free card lists 2 free Agent Builds alongside its 200 credits.

Runs are cheap but not deterministic in cost. Run 1 used 21 credits in 1 minute 56 seconds; run 2, the same Bot on the same 20 pages, used 27 credits in 3 minutes 12 seconds. Identical output, 29% more credits and 65% more wall time. At Basic's 10,000 credits for $13 a month on yearly billing, a run of this size is roughly three cents, so the variance is small in money and worth knowing about in budgeting.

The meter is honest at the account level and confusing at the task level. Balance went 1,500 to 1,222 after the build, 1,201 after run 1 and 1,174 after run 2, which reconciles exactly with the per-task figures in the history list. But the task detail panel showed 'Credits used: 0' for a run that the history list, seconds later, priced at 21. Trust the list and the balance, not the panel.

The agent made one silent design decision. The prompt said 'the first 20 books', and the Bot was built with no parameters and 'first 20' hard-coded; it says so in its own summary and offers to change it on request. Fine for this test, but a Bot you intend to reuse should be built with the count as an input, and you have to ask for that.

Historical: on 4 September the app and the website showed different prices. On first login the app opened a '7-days free trial' panel listing Basic at $16, Essential at $70 and Advanced at $120 a month, with $20, $100 and $200 struck through, while the public pricing page, read the day before, still charged $20, $100 and $200 monthly. That gap closed by 13 September: the public page now shows the same $16, $70 and $120.
not_tested: books.toscrape.com is a static sandbox with no login, no JavaScript rendering and no anti-bot measures, so none of the managed-browser, proxy or CAPTCHA infrastructure in BrowserAct's pitch was exercised. It proves the no-code loop from plain prompt to reusable Bot; it says nothing about hostile sites, where proxy use starts to matter -- free in the cloud for a limited time, 5,000 credits per gigabyte of dynamic proxy traffic on the Local CLI.
sessions.note: Findings as written up after the session; no pass/fail per task was scored.

sessions.what: On 26 September 2026 we built the same class-booking web app in Lovable, Replit and Emergent from one identical prompt, each on its free plan, and checked every result against 18 tests we wrote down before the first build. We changed no code: the builder only got our prompt. Lovable paid us nothing when we ran the test; it accepted us into its affiliate programme on 28 September 2026, and these findings were recorded before that.
findings: Lovable built and published the app in about ten minutes and used 4 of the 10 credits on a new account. It asked twice, to create the project and to publish, and published to a lovable.app address that stays online on the free plan with an 'Edit with Lovable' badge.

It was the only one of the three whose first version held the limit when ten people booked an eight-spot class at the same moment: eight accepted, two refused with 'Sorry, this class is full.' The other two accepted all ten.

It checked input on the server as well as in the form (a name of only spaces and a bad email were refused), kept the admin password out of the page and scripts, and prefixed CSV values starting with = + - or @ so a spreadsheet does not run them as formulas.
It needed no repair round. After republishing, every test booking was still there.

Taking the code with you works, taking the running app does not. With GitHub connected (access limited to one repository), Lovable created its own repository with the full source and database migrations and committed no secret keys. Outside Lovable, on Node 22, it installed and built without errors, but loaded no classes: the database service key and admin password stay in Lovable, so moving means setting up your own database and bringing the bookings as a CSV or Lovable's full database export.
sessions.not_tested: One run on one day on the free plan. Not a security audit or a load test, we did not measure how fast the 20 monthly Cloud credits run down, and we did not trigger Lovable's full database export.
